Choose a mission you can complete successfully, then add the evidence to your course website. You do not need to finish the hardest hardware project to show strong computer-engineering learning.

## Start here for the final part of the course

:::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}
### 1. Save with Git

Make one local Git repository and one useful commit. This works without Wi-Fi.

[Complete Git First Save](projects/git-first-save.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}
### 2. Build your course website

Open the starter, choose the simple `core` version, edit the home page, and render it locally.

[Build Your Course Website](projects/quarto-course-site.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}
### 3. Choose one mission

Pick a Ready mission first. Add its calculation, code, test, photograph, or result to the website.

[Compare the missions](#mission-stats){.btn .btn-primary}
:::

::::

::: {.callout-tip title="A good finish is better than an unfinished giant project"}
A completed foundation, Linux, Python, networking, or documentation mission counts. Start with a minimum result you can demonstrate. Add an extension only after the minimum result works.
:::

## How every mission works

The missions use one repeatable lab pattern. It combines the useful progression found in Grob-style electronics work, Open Circuits resources, software documentation, simulation, and real measurement without requiring every mission to use every tool.

:::: {.mission-paths}
::: {}
### 1. Identify

Find the exact part number, rating, pinout, command, or file. Do not guess.
:::
::: {}
### 2. Predict

Say what should happen. Calculate an expected value when the mission includes a circuit.
:::
::: {}
### 3. Represent

Use a schematic, wiring diagram, flowchart, state table, or command sequence.
:::
::: {}
### 4. Simulate

Test the idea in Tinkercad, Jupyter, or another suitable tool when one is available.
:::
::: {}
### 5. Build

Work one stage at a time. Stop for the required teacher check before power.
:::
::: {}
### 6. Measure

Record a voltage, resistance, current, time, output, or test result with units.
:::
::: {}
### 7. Troubleshoot

Compare expected and actual behaviour. Isolate one cause and record the correction.
:::
::: {}
### 8. Improve

Add one useful extension only after the minimum version works.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note title="Minimum successful submission"}
Identify the exact system, make the minimum version work safely, measure or test one result, and add the evidence to the course website with a Git checkpoint.
:::

## Hardware already available

| Equipment group | Known classroom hardware | How it is used |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Computers | approximately 23 Raspberry Pi 4 computers, several BeagleBones, microSD cards, monitors, keyboards, and mice | Linux, Python, GPIO, logging, state machines, Git, and documentation |
| Core circuits | breadboards, prototyping shields, jumper wires, resistors, LEDs, pushbuttons, capacitors, buzzers, and multimeters | foundation and low-current missions |
| Power | 5 V and 12 V computer supplies plus low-voltage bench supplies | controller power and separately protected load power |
| Motion and water | low-voltage DC motors, small pumps, water sensors, and salvaged mechanisms | motor, pump, warning, and reverse-engineering missions |
| Lighting and automotive | LEDs, LED strip, trailer lamps, relays, fuses, and an automotive horn | indicator, driver, relay, KCL, KVL, and troubleshooting missions |

::: {.callout-note title="Check an unknown part before power"}
Record the label and verify voltage, current, polarity, connector pinout, and required driver before powering a motor, pump, buzzer, LED strip, relay, or salvaged assembly.
:::

## Availability labels

1. **Ready:** begin independently using confirmed low-voltage equipment or software.
2. **Simulation first:** prove the program or circuit logic before physical construction.
3. **Input, driver, or part check:** the teacher confirms the connection and exact component.
4. **Shared station:** use a teacher-prepared setup such as the 12 V relay and trailer lamp.
5. **Optional online:** complete only when accounts, internet access, and privacy approval are available.

## Common mission finish line

Every completed mission needs only the evidence that fits the work:

1. a readable schematic, command sequence, diagram, or plan;
2. relevant calculations, code, or configuration;
3. a test result with units or a clear success check;
4. one useful photograph or screenshot when appropriate;
5. one Git commit after the evidence is added to the course website;
6. a safe shutdown and complete equipment return when hardware was issued.

Students may work together on one physical system, but each student maintains their own Git history and course website.

## If you finish early

Choose one extension, improve the instructions for the next group, add a second project page, repair an accessibility problem, or help test a classmate's mission using their stated success check.
